MECA.TITLE: MRE Type Cam Position Sensor Operation

ITEM.PTXT: The MRE type cam position sensor consists of a magnet and a sensor circuit (IC) with a built-in MRE.

In the MRE type cam position sensor, the rotation of the timing rotor changes the magnetic vector (direction of the magnetic field) applied to the MRE in the cam position sensor, which changes the internal resistance of the MRE. This resistance change is converted to voltage, and the output waveform is compared with a threshold value and shaped into a rectangular wave of Hi (approximately 4V) and Lo (approximately 1V), which is output to the engine control computer. This output signal is compared with the Ne signal to detect the actual camshaft angle and identify cylinders.

By identifying the position of the timing rotor from the voltage output as Hi/Lo digital signals from when the engine is stopped and from pattern recognition of the peak and valley widths of the timing rotor, the crank position at starting can be detected earlier than with the conventional pickup coil type cam position sensor, improving engine startability.
The accelerator position sensor detects the opening angle with 2 systems: a main circuit and a sub circuit. If a malfunction occurs in the signal, the engine control computer switches to limp mode.

ENTRY.PTXT: If a malfunction occurs in either circuit, the engine control computer detects the malfunction from the voltage difference between the main circuit and sub circuit. At this time, a limited accelerator opening angle is calculated from the sensor value of 2 circuit, and throttle control is continued, enabling limp mode driving.
The engine control computer detects the malfunction from the voltages of the main circuit and sub circuit and controls the throttle valve opening angle only within the idling range.

ITEM.PTXT: The throttle position sensor detects the opening angle with 2 systems: a main circuit and a sub circuit. If a malfunction occurs in the signal, the engine control computer switches to limp mode.

ENTRY.PTXT: If a malfunction occurs in either or both circuits, the engine control computer detects the malfunction from the voltage difference between the main circuit and sub circuit. At this time, power to the throttle motor is cut and the throttle valve is returned to a predetermined opening angle by the return spring. Limp mode driving is made possible by controlling engine output using fuel injection control and ignition timing control. Also, even if the engine control computer detects another malfunction such as in the throttle motor, limp mode driving is made possible by performing the above control.

ITEM.PTXT: A compact, lightweight plastic hot-wire type plug-in air flow meter has been adopted. Accordingly, the air cleaner is mounted above the transmission and has been downsized, reducing weight and making it more compact.

The hot-wire type plug-in air flow meter passes part of the intake air through the detection section and directly measures the mass flow rate, improving detection accuracy and reducing intake resistance.

A bypass flow measurement method, which is less affected by intake pulsation from the engine, has been adopted. Also, low loss is achieved by a flow passage structure with low fluid resistance, allowing air volumes from small to large to be measured reliably.

MECA.TITLE: Hot-wire Type Air Flow Meter Operation

ITEM.PTXT: Part of the intake air is bypassed and the intake air volume is measured at the hot wire measuring section. The hot wire measuring section uses a platinum filament (platinum hot wire), and a bridge circuit is formed by the hot wires of the intake air temperature measuring resistor and the heating resistor (heater) to measure the engine intake air volume. Due to the characteristics of the hot-wire type air flow meter, the mass flow rate can in principle be measured directly, so density correction for changes in intake air temperature is not necessary; however, intake air temperature information is required for engine controls such as EFI. Therefore, a compact thermistor type intake air temperature sensor is built into the air flow meter to detect the intake air temperature.

When the intake air volume changes, the bridge circuit of the hot wire measuring section feedback-controls the power supplied to the heating resistor so that the temperature difference between the intake air temperature measuring resistor and the heating resistor (heater) is always kept constant. This supplied power is converted into a voltage and output to the engine control computer. The engine control computer calculates the engine intake air volume from the predetermined relationship between the air flow meter output voltage and flow rate.

The timing rotor on the crankshaft has 34 signal teeth with 2 teeth missing for top dead center detection. The crank position sensor detects the crank rotation signal every 10° and can accurately detect top dead center from the missing teeth area.

As the crankshaft rotates, the air gap between the timing rotor protrusions and the crank position sensor changes, so the magnetic flux passing through the coil of the crank position sensor increases and decreases, generating an electromotive force in the coil. Because this generated voltage is reversed when the timing rotor protrusion approaches and moves away from the cam position sensor, it appears as an AC voltage.

Installed between the three-way catalysts, it converts the oxygen concentration in the exhaust gas into an electromotive force and detects whether the air-fuel ratio is richer or leaner than the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio.
The sensor (zirconia element) is heated by the built-in heater to keep the zirconia element temperature constant and promote feedback control.

An A/F sensor has been adopted to reliably feed back the air-fuel ratio condition from the exhaust gas. A laminated sensor structure has been adopted to promote early activation of the sensor, achieving air-fuel ratio feedback control from immediately after engine start.

The A/F sensor detects and outputs whether the air-fuel ratio is richer or leaner than the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio, O2sensor, the A/F sensor has output characteristics proportional to the air-fuel ratio, enabling the engine control computer to perform more precise air-fuel ratio control.

To activate the A/F sensor, the sensor (zirconia element) must be heated. While a cup type sensor requires time to activate because it is heated indirectly through an atmospheric layer, a laminated type sensor heats the zirconia element directly, shortening the sensor activation time. In addition, the heat mass has been reduced by downsizing the zirconia element.
The sensor is mounted on the exhaust manifold upstream of the three-way catalyst.

A non-contact type accelerator position sensor has been adopted, using a Hall element that can extract the magnetic field strength as an electrical signal using the Hall effect, which provides an output voltage linear to the accelerator pedal depression amount. When the accelerator pedal depression amount changes, the angle of the magnetic field relative to the flow of the applied current in the Hall element changes, so the strength of the magnetic field perpendicular to the applied current changes. The resulting change in voltage, generated perpendicular to both the applied current and the magnetic field, is sent to the engine control computer as the accelerator pedal depression amount signal. In addition, reliability is ensured by adopting a 2-system (main and sub) sensor with different output characteristics.

A 12-hole ultra-fine atomization fuel injector has been adopted. The injector is mounted directly on the cylinder head, and the tip of the fuel injector protrudes into the intake port, shortening the distance to the combustion chamber.
